provenance.note: 04 Amoebiasis.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Badre Eddine Lmimouni)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Only Entamoeba histolytica is pathogenic among the 9 human gut amoebae.
90% asymptomatic, 10% disease; 3rd parasitic cause of death.
Histolytica form: 20-40 µm, haematophagous, invasive.
Minuta: commensal; cyst (4 nuclei): infective, chlorine-resistant.
Faecal-oral (water, raw vegetables, hands) and oral-anal sex.
Short direct (monoxenous) cycle.
Dysentery: mucus + blood without faeces, épreintes, tenesmus.
Liver abscess within 5 months in 95%: Fontan triad, anchovy-sauce pus.
Intestinal: 3 stool exams; visceral: ELISA serology.
Tissue amoebicide (metronidazole) then contact amoebicide (paromomycin).
Aspirate or drain large abscesses.

deeper.title: Why two different amoebicides are needed
deeper.html:
Metronidazole is absorbed and reaches high levels in the gut wall and liver, killing invasive trophozoites, but little remains in the colonic lumen where minuta forms and cysts persist. Without a luminal agent like paromomycin, the patient stays a cyst carrier and can relapse or infect others.

Source: the lecture's treatment slides.

deeper.title: Why stool is often negative in a liver abscess
deeper.html:
By the time an abscess forms, the intestinal episode may be months old and amoebae may no longer be shed in stool. The parasite is now in the liver, beyond the reach of a stool exam. That is why visceral amoebiasis is diagnosed by serology and imaging, not coprology.

Source: the lecture's biological diagnosis slide.

figure.caption: From cyst to dysentery and liver abscess. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Liver abscess: Fontan triad, anchovy-sauce pus

provenance.note: 2 Aspergillosis.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Badre Eddine Lmimouni)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Aspergillus: ubiquitous mould, septate hyaline hyphae; A. fumigatus 90%.
Infection by inhaling conidia; construction works cause hospital outbreaks.
Risk: neutropenia < 500 for > 10 days, corticosteroids, cavities (TB).
Allergic forms: asthma (IgE), ABPA, extrinsic allergic alveolitis (precipitins).
ABPA: eosinophilia > 1000, high total IgE, mucous plugs.
Aspergilloma: fungus ball in a cavity; air-crescent sign; surgery.
IPA: fever resistant to antibiotics > 4 days in neutropenia; CT halo sign.
Galactomannan antigen: early marker; confirm on a 2nd sample; false positives with pip-tazo.
IA classified as proven, probable or possible.
Voriconazole is the reference treatment of IPA; fluconazole inactive.
Prevention: sterile rooms, HEPA filters, posaconazole prophylaxis.

deeper.title: Why neutropenia is the key risk for invasive aspergillosis
deeper.html:
Macrophages kill inhaled conidia, but once conidia germinate into hyphae, neutrophils are the cells that destroy them. With fewer than 500 neutrophils for more than about ten days, hyphae grow unopposed into lung tissue and blood vessels, causing infarcts and haemorrhage, which is what the CT halo sign shows.

Source: the lecture's defences and IPA slides.

deeper.title: Why galactomannan changed the diagnosis
deeper.html:
Cultures and biopsies are slow or too risky in thrombocytopenic patients. Galactomannan is shed by growing Aspergillus into the blood, so twice-weekly screening can flag invasive infection days before symptoms or CT changes. Starting treatment earlier directly improves survival, as the lecture stresses: early diagnosis, better prognosis.

Source: the lecture's galactomannan slides.

figure.caption: Allergy, colonisation of a cavity, invasion. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Aspergilloma: fungus ball in a TB cavity
GM antigen, direct exam, culture, CT

provenance.note: 12 Bilharzia.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Mourad Bouchrik)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Schistosomes: blood flukes with separate sexes in venous plexuses.
'Bare feet' disease: cercariae penetrate skin in fresh water.
S. haematobium: urogenital (Bulinus); S. mansoni: intestinal (Biomphalaria).
Morocco: only S. haematobium, south of the Atlas; dams spread it.
Eggs: haematobium terminal spine; mansoni lateral spine.
Granulomas around trapped eggs → fibrosis.
Invasion: fever, allergy, eosinophilia; stool/urine negative; serology.
Haematobium: terminal haematuria, bladder fibrosis, bladder cancer.
Mansoni: liver fibrosis, portal hypertension.
Eggs detectable 6-8 weeks after infection; urine at noon after exercise.
Serology from 15-30 days.
Praziquantel 40 mg/kg in one day (60 for japonicum).

deeper.title: Why dams can cause schistosomiasis
deeper.html:
Dams and irrigation channels create still, warm fresh water where Bulinus and Biomphalaria snails thrive, in places that were previously arid. When people wash, bathe or farm in that water and there are no latrines, the cycle closes quickly. The Ouarzazate outbreak in Morocco is a textbook example of development creating a parasitic disease.

Source: the lecture's Morocco history slide.

deeper.title: Why the worms themselves do little harm
deeper.html:
Adult schistosomes coat themselves with host molecules and live for years in veins without triggering inflammation. The damage comes from their eggs: many never reach the bladder or bowel lumen and lodge in tissues, where each one triggers a granuloma. Thousands of granulomas scar the bladder wall or the liver's portal spaces, causing haematuria, cancer risk or portal hypertension.

Source: the lecture's cycle and granuloma slides.

figure.caption: Skin penetration in fresh water, eggs in urine or stool. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Spined egg in urine or stool
Adult pairs in venous plexus (bladder / gut)

provenance.note: 23 Candidiasis.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Mourad Bouchrik)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Candida albicans: budding yeast, commensal, opportunistic.
Risk: antibiotics, steroids, diabetes, HIV, catheters, moisture, dentures.
Oral thrush (CD4 < 300); oesophageal candidiasis (CD4 < 100).
Vulvovaginal: 75% of women; curd-like white discharge; pregnancy.
Intertrigo: glazed erythema with satellite pustules.
Nail: perionyxis first, fingers of dominant hand.
Invasive: fever > 96 h despite antibiotics in high-risk host.
Direct exam: abundance matters on mucosal samples.
Culture: Sabouraud-chloramphenicol; chromogenic media.
Germ-tube test (3 h serum, 37 °C) identifies C. albicans.
Mannan antigen + antibodies suggest invasive candidiasis.
Local treatment for skin/mouth; fluconazole; echinocandins or amphotericin for invasive.

deeper.title: Why antibiotics cause thrush
deeper.html:
In the mouth, gut and vagina, bacteria compete with Candida for space and nutrients and produce substances that keep it in check. Broad-spectrum antibiotics wipe out these bacteria, and Candida, which is unaffected, multiplies freely and invades the epithelium. Removing the cause, not just adding an antifungal, prevents recurrences.

Source: the lecture's buccal candidiasis and risk factor slides.

deeper.title: Why a positive culture is not always infection
deeper.html:
Candida albicans lives normally on mucosae and in stool, so finding it proves little by itself. What matters is abundance on direct examination, the site (a sterile site such as blood or CSF is always significant), and the clinical picture. That is why the lecture stresses direct examination and antigen testing alongside culture.

Source: the lecture's direct examination slide.

figure.caption: From commensal to superficial and invasive disease. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: C. albicans: commensal of gut and mucosae
Risk: antibiotics, steroids, diabetes, HIV, catheters
Direct exam, Sabouraud, germ tube, mannan

provenance.note: 06 Coccidiosis.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Badre Eddine Lmimouni)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Coccidia: Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora; intracellular in enterocytes.
Cycle: schizogony, gamogony, sporogony; oocyst = infective form.
Cryptosporidium oocysts resist chlorination → waterborne epidemics.
C. hominis (humans), C. parvum (humans + mammals).
Severe chronic cryptosporidiosis in AIDS with CD4 < 100.
Immunocompetent: self-limited watery diarrhoea 1-2 weeks.
Modified Ziehl-Neelsen: red/pink acid-fast oocysts.
Cryptosporidium treatment: ART + nitazoxanide/paromomycin/azithromycin; rehydrate.
Cyclospora: raspberries, basil, travellers; cotrimoxazole.
Isospora: diarrhoea with fever; cotrimoxazole.
Blastocystis: significant if > 5/field; metronidazole.

deeper.title: Why cryptosporidiosis is so dangerous in AIDS
deeper.html:
Clearance of Cryptosporidium depends on CD4 T cells and interferon-γ. When CD4 cells fall below about 100, the parasite keeps cycling through the enterocytes, with endless autoinfection, profuse diarrhoea and spread to the bile ducts. No drug reliably eradicates it, so restoring immunity with antiretrovirals is the real cure.

Source: the lecture's clinical and treatment slides.

deeper.title: Why chlorinated tap water does not stop Cryptosporidium
deeper.html:
Cryptosporidium oocysts have a thick wall that resists chlorine at the doses used for drinking water. Animal faeces washing into rivers and reservoirs can therefore contaminate a treated water supply and cause city-wide outbreaks. Filtration, or boiling at home, is what removes them.

Source: the lecture's Cryptosporidium and water cycle slides.

figure.caption: Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora and Blastocystis. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: 25 Cryptococcose.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Mourad Bouchrik)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Cryptococcus neoformans: encapsulated yeast, pigeon droppings.
Inhalation → silent lung infection → CNS.
AIDS-defining when CD4 < 100; always test for HIV.
Meningoencephalitis: insidious headache, fever, cranial nerve palsies.
Raised ICP: repeated evacuating lumbar punctures.
LP whenever cryptococcosis is found elsewhere.
CSF: clear, high pressure, lymphocytes, low glucose (may be normal in AIDS).
India ink: capsulated yeasts with a halo.
Capsular antigen (latex) in CSF/serum: diagnosis and follow-up.
Culture on Sabouraud without actidione; urease positive.
Amphotericin B + flucytosine 2 weeks, then fluconazole.

deeper.title: Why the capsule matters so much
deeper.html:
The polysaccharide capsule protects Cryptococcus from phagocytosis and dampens the immune response, making it the main virulence factor. It is also what we detect: India ink outlines it as a halo, and the capsular antigen shed into CSF and blood is the most sensitive diagnostic test and a marker for follow-up.

Source: the lecture's pathogen and diagnosis slides.

deeper.title: Why a lumbar puncture is done even without meningeal signs
deeper.html:
Cryptococcal meningitis can be almost silent, especially in AIDS, with only mild headache while the yeast multiplies in the CSF. Finding Cryptococcus in the lung, skin or blood therefore requires a lumbar puncture, because missing CNS involvement would mean undertreating a fatal infection.

Source: the lecture's neuromeningeal and 'what to do' slides.

figure.caption: From pigeon droppings to meningoencephalitis. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: India ink: capsule in CSF pellet

provenance.note: 03 Diagnosis in Parasitology.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Badre Eddine Lmimouni)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Prescribe 3 stool exams a few days apart: one negative excludes nothing.
3-day low-residue diet; no charcoal, oils, barium.
Diarrhoeal stool: examine within 1 hour.
Lugol stains cysts; MIF preserves and stains.
Combine two concentration methods (physical + diphasic, e.g. Ritchie).
Ziehl-Neelsen: Cryptosporidium (red oocysts).
Baermann: Strongyloides larvae; Kato: egg count; scotch test: pinworm.
Thin smear: species identification and parasitaemia.
Thick drop: WHO reference for malaria.
Sample Plasmodium at fever peaks.
Serology: 2 techniques, 2 samples 15 days apart.
IgM early (no placenta); IgG later, crosses placenta.

deeper.title: Why one negative stool exam proves little
deeper.html:
Parasites shed eggs and cysts intermittently and unevenly through the stool, and a microscopist examines only a tiny sample. A single negative result can simply mean an unlucky day. Three samples on different days, each with two concentration methods, raise sensitivity enough to be useful.

Source: the lecture's introduction and key points slides.

deeper.title: Why the thick drop and thin smear are used together
deeper.html:
The thick drop lyses red cells and piles up many layers of blood, so it finds scanty parasites; but the lysis distorts them, making species identification hard. The thin smear keeps red cells intact, showing the parasite's shape, stage and effect on the red cell, and allows counting parasitaemia. Together they detect and identify.

Source: the lecture's blood research methods slides.

figure.caption: Stool, blood and immunological methods. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Special: Ziehl (Cryptosporidium), Kato, Baermann, scotch test
Thick drop: WHO reference for malaria
Serology: IgM early, IgG late; 2 techniques, 2 samples

provenance.note: 11 Distomatose.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. M. Bouchrik)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Flukes: leaf-shaped trematodes, 2 suckers, no anus, hermaphrodite.
Indirect cycle; intermediate host = freshwater snail.
Operculated, non-embryonated eggs.
Infection by eating metacercariae on wild watercress/dandelion.
Fasciola hepatica: sheep and cattle; humans accidental.
Snail: Lymnaea truncatula.
Invasion (1-4 weeks): toxi-infectious hepatitis; state (3 months): cholangitis.
Eggs in stool only from ~3 months; serology from 3 weeks.
Paragonimus (lung fluke) mimics TB.
Dicrocoelium eggs in stool may be simple transit.
Prevention: avoid wild watercress and raw fish.

deeper.title: Why serology comes before stool in fasciolosis
deeper.html:
During the invasion phase the young flukes are migrating through the liver and are not yet adults, so no eggs are laid. The stool exam stays negative for about three months, while antibodies appear from about three weeks. Serology is therefore the test that can diagnose the acute, symptomatic phase.

Source: the lecture's diagnostic slides.

deeper.title: Why wild watercress is the classic source
deeper.html:
Infected sheep and cattle contaminate wet pastures with eggs; the snails that host the larvae live in the same damp ground, and the cercariae encyst on plants growing in that water. Wild watercress picked near grazing land therefore carries metacercariae, whereas cultivated watercress grown in controlled water does not.

Source: the lecture's large liver fluke slides.

figure.caption: From sheep to snail to watercress. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Adult in bile ducts (sheep, cattle, human)

provenance.note: 05 Flagellates.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Badre Eddine Lmimouni)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Only Giardia is pathogenic among intestinal flagellates.
Giardia: duodenum/jejunum; commonest non-bacterial diarrhoea; young children.
Trophozoite: 2 nuclei, 4 pairs of flagella; cyst: 4 nuclei, infective.
Villous atrophy → fat and B12 malabsorption, steatorrhoea, failure to thrive.
90% asymptomatic carriers.
Diagnosis: 3 stool exams; duodenal aspirate/biopsy if negative.
Metronidazole, or single-dose tinidazole/secnidazole; control stool at 10 days.
Trichomonas vaginalis: no cyst, STI, undulating membrane.
Frothy greenish foul discharge, pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia.
Fresh saline exam: motile, rotating parasite.
Treat both partners with metronidazole.

deeper.title: Why Giardia causes fatty diarrhoea without blood
deeper.html:
Giardia does not invade the mucosa as E. histolytica does; it clings to the surface of the small bowel, flattening the villi and removing the brush border enzymes. The gut can no longer absorb fats and fat-soluble vitamins, so stools become greasy, pale and foul, but there are no ulcers, so no blood.

Source: the lecture's pathophysiology slide.

deeper.title: Why both partners must be treated for Trichomonas
deeper.html:
Men are often asymptomatic carriers in the urethra or prostate. Treating only the symptomatic woman leaves the reservoir untouched, and she is reinfected at the next contact. Treating both partners at once breaks this ping-pong transmission.

Source: the lecture's prevention and therapeutic slide.

figure.caption: Morphology, disease and treatment. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Giardia trophozoite: pear, 2 nuclei, 4 pairs of flagella

provenance.note: Hookworm and Strongyloides.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Mourad Bouchrik)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Hookworms and Strongyloides infect through the skin (bare feet, mud).
Ancylostoma duodenale: 2 pairs of hook teeth; blood-sucking in duodenum.
Hookworm → microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia.
Larval lung migration → Löffler syndrome, eosinophilia.
Hookworm treatment: albendazole 400 mg single dose + iron and folate.
Strongyloides: parthenogenetic female in duodenum.
Autoinfection → persistence 30+ years, saw-tooth eosinophilia.
Larva currens: fast-moving sinuous skin cords.
Malignant strongyloidiasis on corticosteroids: disseminated, fatal.
Diagnosis: rhabditoid larvae in stool; Baermann method.
Treatment: ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose.

deeper.title: Why steroids can make strongyloidiasis fatal
deeper.html:
Strongyloides can complete its cycle without leaving the body, and the immune system normally keeps this autoinfection at a low level for decades. Corticosteroids suppress that control, so larvae multiply unchecked, cross the gut wall carrying bacteria and spread to every organ. That is why people from endemic areas with eosinophilia should be tested and treated before long-term steroids.

Source: the lecture's malignant anguillulosis slide.

deeper.title: Why hookworm causes anaemia
deeper.html:
Each adult hookworm clamps onto the duodenal mucosa with its teeth and sucks blood, moving to new sites and leaving small bleeding points. Hundreds of worms mean a steady daily blood and iron loss, producing microcytic hypochromic anaemia, especially in children and pregnant women with poor iron intake. Treatment must therefore combine a dewormer with iron.

Source: the lecture's hookworm definition and treatment slides.

figure.caption: Hookworms and Strongyloides. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Hookworm in duodenum: blood-sucking → iron-deficiency anaemia

provenance.note: Hydatidosis.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Mourad Bouchrik)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Echinococcus granulosus: adult in dog's intestine; larva forms the hydatid cyst.
Dog = definitive host; sheep = intermediate host; human = accidental dead end.
Infection: stroking dogs, eggs on vegetables/water.
Morocco: stray dogs, clandestine and festival slaughter, offal to dogs.
Cyst layers: pericyst (host), ectocyst, germinal endocyst (brood capsules).
Liver 50-60%, lung 30-40%, kidney 1.5-5%.
Rupture → anaphylaxis or secondary echinococcosis; lung → vomica.
Ultrasound is key: WHO-IWGE CE1-CE5.
Serology: ELISA + HAI screen; Western blot 17 kDa confirms; negative doesn't exclude.
Surgery (90% cure), PAIR, or albendazole; watch-and-wait for CE4-5.
Prevention: deworm dogs with praziquantel, destroy offal.

deeper.title: Why offal is the heart of the problem
deeper.html:
Dogs are infected only by eating organs containing hydatid cysts. Each time sheep liver or lungs from home, festival or clandestine slaughter are thrown to dogs, the cycle is renewed and thousands of eggs are spread onto pastures and gardens. Destroying offal and deworming dogs breaks the cycle at its most vulnerable point.

Source: the lecture's epidemiology and prophylaxis slides.

deeper.title: Why a ruptured cyst is dangerous twice over
deeper.html:
Hydatid fluid is full of parasite antigens; when a cyst ruptures, the sudden release can cause an anaphylactic reaction. And the protoscolices it contains are alive: each one can grow into a new cyst wherever it lands, causing secondary echinococcosis. That is why surgeons sterilise the cyst before opening it and give albendazole around the procedure.

Source: the lecture's cyst structure and complications slides.

figure.alt: Echinococcus granulosus cycle and the hydatid cyst
figure.caption: Dog, sheep and the accidental human host. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Cyst: pericyst, ectocyst, germinal layer, sand

provenance.note: 01 General Introduction.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Badre Eddine Lmimouni)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Parasite: eukaryote living at a host's expense.
Protozoa (unicellular) vs metazoa (helminths, arthropods).
Helminths: nematodes, cestodes, trematodes.
Parasitism vs commensalism vs symbiosis.
Dead end: unusual host, no adult stage (larva migrans, hydatid cyst in humans).
Ectoparasite → infestation; endoparasite → infection.
Entry: ingestion, skin (Schistosoma), transplacental (Toxoplasma), bite (Plasmodium).
Definitive host = adult/sexual; intermediate host = larval/asexual.
Direct short (amoeba), direct long (Ancylostoma), indirect (Taenia).
Pinworm: evening anal itch, scotch test, albendazole repeated at 15-21 days.

deeper.title: Why the cycle is the key to every parasitosis
deeper.html:
Each step of a cycle is a place where the parasite can be found or stopped. Where it exits tells you which sample to test (stool, urine, sputum); where it enters tells you how to prevent it (wash vegetables, avoid fresh water, use nets); and which hosts it needs tells you where to break transmission (treat dogs for hydatid disease, control snails for bilharzia).

Source: the lecture's importance of the life cycle slide.

deeper.title: Why pinworm treatment is repeated
deeper.html:
Albendazole kills adult worms but not all eggs, and a child re-infects themselves by scratching and swallowing eggs. The second dose 2-3 weeks later kills the worms that hatched in the meantime, and treating the household and washing bedding stops the loop.

Source: the lecture's oxyurosis example.

figure.caption: Monoxenous, heteroxenous and dead-end cycles. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Direct short: one host, no outside maturation (amoeba)
Direct long: one host, maturation in soil (Ancylostoma)
Dead end: accidental host (hydatid cyst, larva migrans)

provenance.note: 09 Leishmaniasis.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Badre Eddine Lmimouni)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Leishmania: flagellate, obligate intracellular in macrophages.
Vector: female sandfly (Phlebotomus); painful night bite.
Promastigote in fly; amastigote in mammals.
Reservoirs: dog (L. infantum), rodents (L. major), human (L. tropica).
Notifiable in Morocco since 1995.
VL (L. infantum): child, fever + pallor + splenomegaly, pancytopenia, ↑ gammaglobulins.
VL diagnosis: bone marrow amastigotes; rK39; ELISA/WB.
L. tropica: urban, dry, single slow lesion. L. major: rural, wet, multiple, fast.
Mucocutaneous (L. braziliensis): nose/palate destruction.
Glucantime: intralesional (< 5 lesions, < 4 cm) or IM 20 mg/kg/d.
VL: antimony 28 days or liposomal amphotericin B.
Monitor ECG (QT) on antimony.

deeper.title: Why leishmaniasis targets macrophages
deeper.html:
Promastigotes are taken up by macrophages, the very cells meant to kill them, and survive by transforming into amastigotes that resist digestion inside the phagolysosome. They multiply there and spread with these cells to the spleen, liver and bone marrow in visceral disease, which is why marrow puncture finds them and why the spleen enlarges.

Source: the lecture's life cycle slides.

deeper.title: Why L. tropica and L. major behave differently
deeper.html:
L. tropica circulates between humans in towns, producing a single, dry, slow lesion. L. major lives in rural rodents and infects people who enter their habitat; the lesions are multiple and very inflamed but heal faster. Knowing the reservoir explains the setting, the lesion type and the control measures (rodent control vs treating human cases).

Source: the lecture's cutaneous leishmaniasis slides.

figure.caption: Sandfly, forms and clinical pictures. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: 07 Malaria.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Badre Eddine Lmimouni)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Plasmodium via female Anopheles (bites 11 p.m.-4 a.m.).
241 million cases, 627,000 deaths (2020); Africa 95%; falciparum 99%.
Morocco: malaria-free certified in 2010; cases are imported.
Falciparum: tertian, deadliest, cerebral malaria, no relapse after 2 months.
Vivax/ovale: hypnozoites → late relapses; malariae: quartan (72 h).
Any fever after travel to an endemic area = malaria until proven otherwise.
Uncomplicated: incubation 7-21 days, fever, chills, sweats; thrombocytopenia.
Severe: coma, seizures, Hb < 7, acidosis, renal failure, parasitaemia ≥ 4%.
Diagnosis within 2 h: thick drop + thin smear; RDT never alone.
Falciparum: artemether-lumefantrine 3 days; vivax/ovale: chloroquine + primaquine.
Severe: IV artesunate in ICU.
Prevention: nets, repellents, chemoprophylaxis, vector control.

deeper.title: Why falciparum is the killer
deeper.html:
P. falciparum invades red cells of any age, so parasitaemia can rise very high, and it places adhesive proteins on the red cell surface that make infected cells stick to capillary walls. These cells pile up in the brain, kidneys and lungs, blocking flow and causing the organ failure of severe malaria. The other species infect a limited pool of red cells and do not sequester in this way.

Source: the lecture's cytoadherence and cerebral malaria slides.

deeper.title: Why vivax needs primaquine
deeper.html:
Chloroquine clears the parasites in the blood, but P. vivax and P. ovale leave dormant hypnozoites in the liver that can wake months later and cause a new attack. Primaquine is the drug that kills these liver forms; because it can cause haemolysis, G6PD status must be checked first.

Source: the lecture's species and Moroccan treatment protocol slides.

figure.caption: Liver, red cells and the mosquito. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Red cells: ring → trophozoite → schizont → merozoites

provenance.note: 24 Malassezioses.pdf (Parasitology and Mycology, Pr. Mourad Bouchrik)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Malassezia: lipophilic, keratinophilic commensal yeast of sebaceous skin.
Benign but recurrent; peak age 18-40; summer, sweating, oils.
Hormonal factors: Cushing's, pregnancy, contraceptives, steroids.
Forms: pityriasis versicolor, dandruff, seborrhoeic dermatitis, folliculitis.
Versicolor: round scaly macules on trunk, chip sign, later achromic.
Wood's lamp: yellow-green fluorescence.
Scotch test: 'bunch of grapes' spores + short filaments.
Culture not needed.
Not contagious; depigmentation persists after cure.
Topical azoles 2-3 weeks or ketoconazole gel once; systemic if diffuse/recurrent.

deeper.title: Why pityriasis versicolor leaves pale spots
deeper.html:
Malassezia produces substances (such as azelaic acid) that inhibit melanocytes in the infected skin, so the patches stop tanning. When the fungus is killed, the melanocytes need weeks to months to recover, which is why the white spots persist after a successful treatment and why patients must be warned not to mistake this for failure.

Source: the lecture's patient information slide.

deeper.title: Why relapse is the rule
deeper.html:
Malassezia is part of normal skin flora and cannot be eradicated. The disease reflects local conditions (sweat, sebum, heat, hormones) that let it overgrow. As long as those conditions return, for example each summer, the rash tends to come back, which is why prophylactic shampoos and patient education matter as much as the first treatment.

Source: the lecture's definition and patient information slides.

exam_points: Pinworm: short direct cycle, eggs embryonated at laying → autoinfestation.
Pinworm eggs laid at the anus at night: evening anal itch, scotch test.
Albendazole repeated at 15-21 days + household measures.
Ascaris: largest (up to 35 cm), small intestine; eggs mature in soil.
Ascaris larvae migrate through lungs: Löffler syndrome, eosinophilia.
Ascaris: no autoinfestation; eggs mamillated.
Adults in 8-12 weeks (Ascaris); 2-4 weeks (pinworm).
Whipworm eggs: lemon-shaped with 2 polar plugs.
Heavy whipworm: dysentery, rectal prolapse, iron-deficiency anaemia.
Treatment: albendazole or mebendazole.

deeper.title: Why pinworm keeps coming back
deeper.html:
Pinworm eggs are infective as soon as they are laid, on the skin around the anus. Scratching puts them under the nails and on bedding, and they are swallowed or inhaled again within days. That is why one dose is not enough and why the whole household, hands, nails and bedding must be treated at the same time.

Source: the lecture's pinworm cycle and treatment slides.

deeper.title: Why Ascaris causes a cough before a stomach ache
deeper.html:
Swallowed Ascaris larvae do not stay in the gut at first: they cross into the blood, pass through the liver and lodge in the lungs, where they grow before being coughed up and swallowed again. This lung passage causes Löffler syndrome with eosinophilia weeks before adult worms settle in the intestine and eggs appear in the stool.

Source: the lecture's Ascaris cycle slide.

exam_points: Pneumocystis jirovecii: opportunistic fungus; airborne; human reservoir.
First AIDS complication before ART; CD4 < 200.
Also steroids, chemotherapy, transplants, haemopathies, prematurity.
Dyspnoea, dry cough, fever, hypoxaemia; auscultation often normal.
Pneumonia not improving on usual antibiotics in an immunocompromised host.
CT: bilateral ground-glass.
Raised LDH; hypoxaemia.
Cannot be cultured: BAL with Grocott/MGG or PCR.
Cotrimoxazole 21 days; steroids if PaO₂ < 70 mmHg.
Prophylaxis: cotrimoxazole if CD4 < 200; stop when > 200 for 3 months.

deeper.title: Why steroids help in severe pneumocystosis
deeper.html:
When cotrimoxazole kills the organisms, their breakdown triggers a burst of lung inflammation that can worsen hypoxaemia in the first days of treatment. Corticosteroids blunt this reaction, which is why they reduce deaths and the need for ventilation in patients who are already hypoxaemic (PaO₂ below 70 mmHg).

Source: the lecture's corticotherapy slide.

deeper.title: Why cotrimoxazole prophylaxis matters so much
deeper.html:
Before prophylaxis and antiretroviral therapy, Pneumocystis pneumonia was the commonest AIDS-defining illness. A single daily tablet of cotrimoxazole when CD4 fall below 200 largely prevents it, and also protects against toxoplasmosis, making it one of the most effective interventions in HIV care.

Source: the lecture's prophylaxis slide and the toxoplasmosis lecture.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: T. gondii: obligate intracellular coccidian; cats are definitive hosts.
Humans are intermediate hosts and a dead end.
Tachyzoite: acute, crosses placenta; cyst (bradyzoites): chronic; oocyst: cats only.
Cysts destroyed at 50 °C for 30 min or −20 °C for 24 h.
Infection: undercooked meat, oocysts (vegetables, water, cat litter), transplacental.
1st trimester: rare transmission, severe damage; 3rd: frequent, mild.
Immunocompetent: 80% silent; cervical nodes.
Congenital severe: hydrocephalus, calcifications, chorioretinitis.
Serology: IgG + IgM; avidity dates infection (> 0.5 = > 4 months).
Seronegative pregnant women: monthly serology + hygiene advice.
Antenatal diagnosis: PCR on amniotic fluid.
Spiramycin (no fetal infection) vs pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine (infected fetus).
AIDS: cotrimoxazole prophylaxis if CD4 < 100.

deeper.title: Why early pregnancy infection is rarer but worse
deeper.html:
In early pregnancy the placenta is small and a better barrier, so fewer parasites reach the fetus. When they do, they strike organs that are still forming, causing major brain and eye lesions or abortion. Late in pregnancy the placenta lets parasites through easily, but the fetus is mature and receives maternal antibodies at the same time, so lesions are milder or latent.

Source: the lecture's pathophysiology slide.

deeper.title: Why IgM alone cannot date an infection
deeper.html:
IgM normally marks a recent infection, but in toxoplasmosis it can persist for months or years at low levels. A woman with IgG and IgM may therefore have been infected long before pregnancy. Avidity testing solves this: antibodies bind more strongly as the response matures, so high avidity means the infection is at least four months old.

Source: the lecture's serology and avidity slides.
